memoryText: I have loved you with an everlasting love; therefore I have continued my faithfulness to you.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Jeremiah 31:3 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
This verse stands at the front of the great chapter of the new covenant. It is spoken to a people who have just lost everything. They had broken the covenant, and the covenant curses had fallen. Here is what God says first: “I have loved you.”

“I have loved you with an everlasting love.” The word “everlasting” goes back before time and extends beyond it. It is not a love that began when Israel obeyed or ended when they failed. It was there before they did anything. Paul says the same of believers: God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world. His love is not based on our performance.

“Therefore I have continued my faithfulness to you.” The word “therefore” is important. Because of his love, he continues to be faithful. The word for “continued” means to draw out or extend, like drawing a long line. God has stretched his faithfulness over the whole history of their rebellion. He has not given up. Judgment was a form of faithfulness to the covenant, and the promise of restoration is too.

Think of the context. The exiles heard this in Babylon. They might have thought that God’s love had ended with the destruction of the temple. This verse says no. The love is everlasting. The exile does not change it.

For the Christian, the cross is the proof. “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” Romans 8:38-39 says that nothing can separate us from the love of God. Say this verse whenever you doubt that you are loved.
weekInReview: This week you read the heart of Jeremiah: the Book of Consolation. You read the promise of a new covenant, in which God will write his law on the hearts of his people, bring them all to know him, and forgive their sin and remember it no more. You read of Jeremiah’s purchase of a field while the Babylonians besieged the city, a picture of faith in a future he could not see. You watched King Zedekiah’s fear of men, Jeremiah in the cistern, and Ebed-melech’s courage. You saw the Rechabites keep their vow, and a king burn God’s word in a fire while the word survived. And you finished the first part with the fall of Jerusalem. In the psalms, you prayed Psalm 107, a song for the redeemed from every kind of trouble. The week taught that God keeps his promises even when everything seems lost, and that his love is everlasting.
reflectionQuestions: The new covenant promises that God will write his law on our hearts. What part of obedience still feels like an outward duty to you rather than a desire, and how might you ask God to change that?
Jeremiah bought a field when the city was falling. What step of faith might God be asking you to take toward a future you cannot see?
Psalm 107 asks the redeemed to say so. Whose story of rescue could you tell this week, and who needs to hear it?
prayerPrompts: Thank God for his everlasting love and continued faithfulness.
Thank him for the new covenant in Jesus’ blood.
